title: Game, fish, milk and gardens after fallout
summary: Don’t use milk from your own animals, or wild game and fish, until officials say you can, and don’t pick or eat garden food until they say so (Water and food after fallout). No source opened says when they can be used, and nothing on this page says they are fine. If no official word ever comes, this page gives what older federal civil defence handbooks and federal guidance for agencies say, each named, with its year. For wild game, fish and eggs no source says anything.
doFirst: From Water and food after fallout: “No current source opened says when milk from your own animals, or wild game and fish, can be used after fallout. This app’s caution: treat them like food that was outdoors, and don’t use them until officials say you can.”
From Water and food after fallout: “Don’t pick or eat food from your garden until officials say you can (CDC, Ready.gov).”
When officials do say what can be eaten, do what they say. Nothing on this page overrides them.
Don’t go outside to tend animals or the garden while you are sheltering. When you may go out is in How long to stay in.

blocks.p: Stored food and drinks, water, babies, medicine and pet food after fallout are in Water and food after fallout. This page is only for food that grows, grazes, swims or lays: the garden, milk from your own animals, eggs, wild game and fish, and feed for animals you keep.

Current federal advice (CDC, Ready.gov) says not to eat garden food, or food or liquids that were outdoors and uncovered, until officials say you can. It says nothing about milk, eggs, game or fish. If officials never speak, this page shows what older federal civil defence handbooks say, each named with its year and marked dated, and what federal guidance written for agencies says. None of them tells you a food is fine to eat, and this page never does.

blocks.warn: Don’t pick or eat food from your garden until officials say you can (CDC, Ready.gov).

list: EPA’s planning manual for officials (2017) says the steps after a radiation incident might include limits on eating garden produce or other locally grown food. It gives no rule for a household.

FDA’s recommendations for state and local agencies (1998) name two ways to lower contamination on fresh produce: removing it from the surface by brushing, washing or peeling, and holding the food so its radioactivity can decay. They are written for agencies after a radiation accident, such as at a nuclear power plant, not for fallout from a nuclear explosion, and they give no times or amounts for a household.

The 1968 civil defence handbook In Time of Emergency (dated) says radiation passing through food does not contaminate it; the danger is swallowing fallout particles that are on the food, and those could be wiped or washed off. It does not say when garden food can be eaten.

blocks.p: If no official word ever comes: brushing, washing and peeling are the only steps any source opened names for fresh produce, and no source opened says they make it fine to eat. No source opened says how long to wait before eating from the garden.

No current source opened says when milk from your own cows or goats can be drunk after fallout. Water and food after fallout says: “The 1968 civil defence handbook In Time of Emergency (dated) says that milk from cows that grazed on pasture with fallout on it might harm the thyroid glands of infants and small children, and that, if authorities say the regular milk supply is contaminated, they should have canned or powdered milk for a few weeks.”

list: FDA’s recommendations for agencies (1998) list, as steps to protect milk: taking milking animals off contaminated pasture and feed, putting dairy cows on stored feed, and giving them uncontaminated water in place of contaminated water. These are written for agencies after a radiation accident, not for fallout from a nuclear explosion.
EPA’s planning manual for officials (2017) leaves milk to FDA’s guidance and gives no advice for a household.
No source opened gives a goat-milk rule of its own, and none says how long to wait before drinking milk from your own animals.

blocks.p: Feeding babies and young children after fallout, including formula, is in Water and food after fallout.

sections.h: Animals you keep: shelter, feed and water

blocks.p: FDA’s recommendations for agencies (1998) list these early steps for farm animals after a radiation accident: moving animals to shelter, corralling livestock, and giving them protected feed and water. They also list taking milking and meat animals off contaminated feed and pasture, and giving them uncontaminated water. FDA wrote them for agencies, not for a household, and not for fallout from a nuclear explosion; no current source opened gives farm-animal steps for fallout.
Ready.gov: “If you are instructed to stay inside during a radiation emergency, pets and service animals should be inside too.” Washing a pet that was outside is in Coming in from outside.

blocks.warn: None of this is a reason to go outside while you are sheltering. How long to stay in owns when you may go out.

blocks.p: The 1968 handbook says special advice for rural families on crops and livestock was available from the US Department of Agriculture. This app does not have that advice.

No source opened says anything about eggs from your own hens after fallout: not CDC, Ready.gov, EPA (2017), FDA (1998), or the 1968 and 1985 civil defence handbooks. This app’s caution: treat them like milk from your own animals, and don’t use them until officials say you can.

No source opened says anything about wild game after fallout: not CDC, Ready.gov, EPA (2017), FDA (1998), or the 1968 and 1985 civil defence handbooks. The rule at the top of this page is the only one: don’t use it until officials say you can.

No source opened says anything about eating fish you catch after fallout: not CDC, Ready.gov, EPA (2017), FDA (1998), or the 1968 and 1985 civil defence handbooks. The rule at the top of this page is the only one: don’t use it until officials say you can.
